question_text: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of chest discomfort and progressive dyspnea. He cannot do daily chores without feeling out of breath. He has a history of an X-linked recessive disorder that causes progressive proximal muscle weakness and gait abnormalities. Physical examination shows a waddling gait and weak patellar reflexes. Cardiovascular examination shows a holosystolic murmur, displaced point of maximal impulse, and bilateral pitting edema of the ankle. Laboratory studies show elevated levels of brain natriuretic peptide. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's muscle weakness?

                    ### Question
                    A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of chest discomfort and progressive dyspnea. He cannot do daily chores without feeling out of breath. He has a history of an X-linked recessive disorder that causes progressive proximal muscle weakness and gait abnormalities. Physical examination shows a waddling gait and weak patellar reflexes. Cardiovascular examination shows a holosystolic murmur, displaced point of maximal impulse, and bilateral pitting edema of the ankle. Laboratory studies show elevated levels of brain natriuretic peptide. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's muscle weakness?

opb. Defective lysine-hydroxylysine crosslinking of tropocollagen
opc. Interruption of microtubule depolymerization through stabilization of GDP-tubulin
opd. Cell–mediated cytotoxicity against skeletal muscle antigens in the endomysium
ope. Increased number of CTG repeats in the DMPK gene

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The most likely underlying cause of this patient's muscle weakness is the increased number of CTG repeats in the DMPK gene, leading to myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1). This condition can manifest as progressive muscle weakness, difficulty in daily chores, progressive dyspnea, and ultimately heart failure, which explains the elevated brain natriuretic peptide levels. The patient's symptoms are consistent with heart failure-related muscle weakness associated with DM1.
